A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ready Jurist One, comprising J1-ENVS and J1-EVAL. Their main text, tables, figures, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including the prompts and evaluation checklists.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments evaluating 17 LLM agents, human assessments, repeated simulations, and dialogue-length sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, repeated simulations, human evaluations, failure analyses, and qualitative case studies.

M1.justification: The proposed court-procedure evaluator changes substantially. v1 Appendix D.3 evaluates stage/action completion through matching; v3 introduces dialogue-stage classification followed by semantic LLM checklist evaluation, with stage restrictions, negative defaults, and restrictions on crediting multiple actions per turn. This changes a central J1-EVAL component; the underlying simulation framework remains largely intact.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six Chinese legal scenarios using 508 instances. v1 Table 4 and v3 Table 5 retain counts of 98, 62, 93, 93, 93, and 69. The expanded analyses and replication experiments operate within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: The main 17-model comparison retains its comparator set. In the Qwen-driven environment comparison, however, Gemma3-Instruct-12B and Chatlaw2 are replaced by Qwen3-32B and InternLM3-8B, while GPT-4o, Deepseek-v3, and Qwen3-14B remain. Compare v1 Table 5/Figure 6 with v3 Tables 11–12/Figure 5.

E3.justification: Court procedural scoring changes from matching to staged semantic checklist assessment. Human consistency sampling changes from 10% of cases per scenario to 20 cases, and evaluator validation changes from 10 to 20 cases per scenario. Replication also extends to court scenarios. The stated hardware, greedy decoding, and maximum dialogue-turn budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds process-versus-outcome analysis, four-category court failure analysis, scenario-specific evaluator disagreement analysis, and court/judgment/complaint case studies (Section 4.3; Appendices G.3 and H). Conversely, v1 Appendix F.2's dialogue-turn sensitivity experiment and its civil/criminal court radar plots are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions already report three-run experiments. v3 replaces limited raw per-run tables with mean ± standard deviation reporting for five agents across all six scenarios (Tables 11–12). It also newly documents seven independent human ratings per case and averaging after discarding the highest and lowest ratings. This expands statistical reporting without establishing an increased repeat count.

E6.justification: Court results change extensively: GPT-4o's civil procedural score changes from 64.22 to 87.0 and criminal charge accuracy from 92.75 to 60.9 (v1 Table 2; v3 Table 3). The reported overall leader changes from GPT-4o to Claude-3.7. These are revised results accompanying evaluation changes, not demonstrated same-setting gains. v3 also adds process/outcome summaries and failure frequencies; most Level I/II scores only undergo rounding.

T1.justification: The reported penalty metric specification changes from the explicit absolute log-distance definition in v1 Appendix D.3, Equation 2, to normalized logarithmic deviation bounded to [0,1] in v3 Table 2 and Appendix D.3. The normalization formula is unspecified. The format-following product equation remains unchanged, and neither version develops theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The first dynamic legal benchmark claim, six-scenario scope, 17-agent evaluation, and below-60% headline conclusion remain. A limited headline finding changes: v1 identifies GPT-4o as the strongest model in its abstract and introduction, whereas v3 removes that identification and names Claude-3.7 as strongest in its results.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking procedural competence to valid outcomes, defence-drafting difficulty to counterargument construction, and civil-court evaluator disagreement to longer text and more metrics. Its case studies explain coordination failures, missing legal interpretations, and rigid template copying. The dialogue-length/long-range-memory interpretation is removed, while limitations gain discussion of transfer beyond the Chinese legal system.

D1.justification: v3 adds three simulation algorithms, evaluated-agent prompts, dialogue segmentation and checklist prompts, and detailed human-annotation qualifications, blinding, aggregation, and interface documentation. However, v1's topic-list construction prompts are removed. The project URL on v1's first page is also removed, while v3 promises resources upon acceptance; the PDFs do not establish actual online availability.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to ReAct and the LLM-as-a-Judge survey, while removing AgentGym and Song and Wei's courtroom-emotion study. Its positioning against static legal benchmarks remains substantially the same. Moving existing legal-benchmark and simulation discussion into the main text does not constitute new related-work coverage.

P1.justification: The introduction, environment description, evaluation narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Legal-source construction moves into Section 3, metrics receive outcome/process groupings and numbered identifiers, further analysis becomes a separate subsection, and much related work moves from the appendix into the main text. These are substantial narrative and organizational revisions.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout and combines the scenario overview and construction pipeline into a redesigned Figure 1. It adds a metric-definition table, outcome/process summary columns, failure heatmaps, case-study figures, and annotation screenshots. Replication tables are restructured, sensitivity radar plots disappear, and retained appendix prompts are redistributed and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v3 improves auditability through simulation pseudocode, detailed scoring prompts, broader replication summaries, and documented human assessment. Its failure analyses and case studies also make weaknesses more concrete. These gains are tempered by removed sensitivity and data-construction material, deferred resource access, and unresolved reporting details, including penalty normalization and inconsistent Qwen model attribution in Appendix G.2 versus its tables. The net improvement is useful but limited.
